title: How to Model a Skill Effectively: The I Do Stage of Explicit Teaching
author: Trudy Mayo
summary: Trudy Mayo sets out what makes the I Do stage of explicit teaching effective. She insists modelling is one short, live worked example with the teacher thinking aloud, not a lecture or a finished slide to copy. The example must match the success criteria exactly, and should run about five minutes before an engagement cue. Students' job in this phase is to watch and listen, not write or ask, with norms taught at the start of the year and each term. She recommends a hidden teacher prep notes page showing the completed example so the delivery stays confident and consistent, and a quick one- or two-item check for understanding before moving to We Do. The post closes with a pitch for her paid resource pack, which slightly dilutes it, but the instructional core is substantive.
points: A strong I Do is one brief live worked example that makes the steps visible and keeps cognitive load low.
The model must mirror the success criteria precisely, narrating decisions that link back to them.
Students watch and listen during modelling; attention, not participation, is the goal, and norms need explicit teaching.
A concealed, fully worked prep page lets teachers focus on delivery instead of improvising examples.
A fast check for understanding before We Do tells you whether to proceed or clarify.
quotes: Modelling is one of the most powerful parts of explicit teaching, yet it is also the stage that slips quickest into over-talking, over-explaining or disengaging students. A strong I Do looks deceptively simple.

The worked example should match the success criteria exactly. If the criteria say students will identify three points, your model must show three points. If the criteria say students will use a specific strategy, your model must demonstrate that strategy precisely.

The modelling itself should be short and direct. Most teachers over-talk because they are trying to fill gaps that the worked example will solve on its own. Aim for no more than five minutes before you pause, use an engagement norm or have students track with you. Attention dips quickly, and the goal of the I Do is clarity, not a monologue.

And most importantly, complete the worked example in the moment, in front of the students. A live model is far more effective than a finished (or clicked-through) one. It reduces cognitive load, allows for correction and helps students see the process rather than the product.

During the I Do, students are expected to watch and listen. This is not a time for them to write, ask questions, or attempt the task. Their role is to follow the teacher’s thinking, track each step as it is modelled, and observe how the success criteria are applied in real time. The focus is on attention, not participation.

Before moving into guided practice, you should run one or two quick checks for understanding. This is not a retell of the model or a discussion of the steps. It is a fast, low-effort question to confirm that students recognised the skill you just demonstrated.
